fixes.explanation: That's right. Jesus says, "When you pray, say: 'Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come." (Luke 11:2). The kingdom is in the prayer, but the first thing they call God is Father. That's the first word, baker, and it's a close one.

Jesus is talking to His disciples here, baker, but listen to what He says. He says, "For everyone who asks receives…" (Luke 11:10). The word is everyone, and He doesn't name a smaller group. That's the word to hold onto.

Fasting is a good guess, but this disciple doesn't ask about it. In Luke 11:1 he says, "Lord, teach us to pray…" Prayer is what he brings up after Jesus finishes praying. We'll get to bread soon enough, baker.
Yes, baker. The disciple says, "…just as John taught his disciples." (Luke 11:1). He points to another teacher's students and asks for the same thing. I respect a man who asks for what he wants.
A whole week's worth sounds nice and tidy, friend. But Luke 11:3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread." The word is day, not week. It's one day at a time.
A whole year in one ask? That's a big order, baker. The prayer in Luke 11:3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread." It's a day-sized request, not a year-sized one.

It's actually true, friend, and the story says so. The man tells his friend, "…because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him." (Luke 11:6). That's his reason for asking. One guest, one journey, and nothing to set before him.

What a nice neighbor that would be, friend, but that's not what he says. The friend inside answers, "Do not bother me." (Luke 11:7). "Come on in" isn't anywhere in his answer. That's a different story from the one Jesus tells.
Sending him down the street is a clever move, baker, but the man inside doesn't say that. His first words are, "Do not bother me." (Luke 11:7). He doesn't mention anyone else in that answer.
Stingy isn't how Jesus tells it, friend. Luke 11:8 says the friend "…will get up and give him as much as he needs." The measure is what the man needs, not a number of loaves.

Half sounds like a bargain bin, baker, but that's not in the story. Luke 11:8 says the friend "…will get up and give him as much as he needs." The measure is what the man needs, and half isn't mentioned.

That's the word, baker. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). It's the same word as the shut door in the midnight story, where the friend says, "My door is already shut…" (Luke 11:7). Ask, seek, knock. Easy to remember.

That one sounds big and holy, baker, but it's not the word here. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). The knocking opens a door, the same word as the shut door in the midnight story (Luke 11:7).

That's right, baker. Jesus asks, "What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?" (Luke 11:11-12). He asks these as questions, and He doesn't say fathers do it.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "…how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). The gift He names is the Holy Spirit. The words "…how much more…" are right there.
